issues.title: Do we need RESTCONF depth/fields filters?
issues.author: cabo
issues.body:
(Andy Bierman, <https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/core/XLv4ZusZubBrJPC5aW7UqqeHrxw>)

The client must know all of the key values in advance
before being able to use the SID of a data node
in a FETCH request.  It is difficult and expensive
to retrieve the entire datastore contents at once,
just to discover the key values in use for the YANG list
entries within the datastore.

RESTCONF has the 'depth' and 'fields' filter parameters
to address this issue. NETCONF has subtree and XPath filtering.
NETCONF servers can generally support selection of 1 value or all
values, for each key.

Perhaps CORECONF will need the 'depth' filter parameter.

comments.author: abierman
comments.body:
Follow up: OK to defer to future

- The client does not need to know all the keys in advance to get all the list entries, by getting an ancestor of the list
-  The amount of data retrieved depends on the YANG modules used. It is possible to design containers with limited
   child nodes and depth. It is possible to limit the maximum number of list instances, or expect a small number of entries by design,
-  The 'depth' parameter is not likely to help in CoMI because the data trees will not be as complex or deep as NETCONF
-  These filtering query parameters are optional in RESTCONF

The likely problem is that the list is too wide, not too deep.
Even a simple list with 4 leafs in it is a lot of data if there are 10000 entries in the list.
If needed, a list pagination mechanism could be added in the future.
NETCONF WG has work-in-progress: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-netconf-list-pagination/

comments.author: lemikev
comments.body:
For now, getting indexes, pagination, and other approaches can be implemented using RPCs.
This can be sufficient even for the long term.

Michel

issues.title: »null« is a valid data item in YANG/CBOR; need to do indicate absent/removed nodes differently
issues.author: cabo
issues.body:
null is used in an iPATCH to remove a data node or in a FETCH to indicate the absence of a data node.

However, in RFC 9254 (Encoding of Data Modeled with YANG in CBOR), null is a valid data node value.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9254#section-6.11

This issue has been raised last year and not yet resolved.
The fix consists of replacing all instances of null in draft-ietf-core-comi by undefined.

undefined is CBOR value F7, null is CBOR value F6
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8949#section-5.7

(Via Michel Veillette)

pulls.title: Minimal-change revision for WGLC: drop atomicity, scope out NMDA
pulls.author: apelov
pulls.body:
Minimal-change revision aimed at getting the draft to WGLC: remove transaction /
atomicity semantics, reserve an atomicity extension point, explicitly scope out
NMDA datastore selection, and add the corresponding security note.

Atomicity, NMDA datastore selection, and rich per-item failure reporting are
**deferred to a separate future extension document** (not written here). The
guiding constraint throughout was a minimal diff: 67 insertions, 9 deletions, one
file, confined to the sections listed below plus ToC/section-number mechanics.

One commit per work item, so individual items can be dropped or discussed
separately.

## WI-1 — Remove transaction/atomicity semantics

Sections: §6 Error Handling; §3.2 Data Editing (new §3.2.1 "Request Processing");
§3.2.5 iPATCH; §1 Introduction.

- Removed the all-or-nothing requirement in §6: *"Requests that result in an
  error response MUST NOT have an effect on the datastore."*
- Added the replacement processing model once, in a new "Request Processing"
  subsection: items processed in order; each applied best-effort; partial failure
  permitted with no required revert; error response on failure with remaining
  items MAY stop at first failure; client responsible for constructing consistent
  requests and for detecting/repairing partial application. §6 and iPATCH now
  reference it. First-error reporting only — no per-item result structure.
- Intro: "single editing transaction" → "single editing operation". The sentence
  is about round-trips, not atomicity, so this only removes the
  atomicity-flavoured wording.

## WI-2 — Reserve the atomicity extension point

Section: §3.2 Data Editing (new §3.2.2 "Future processing extensions").

States that requests defined here are best-effort/non-atomic; that future
extensions MAY define stricter (e.g. atomic) semantics; that such semantics MUST
be explicitly signalled in the request (e.g. a CoAP option or a Content-Format
parameter); and that an extension MUST NOT change the semantics of unsignalled
requests. The signal must be defined so that a server which does not recognise it
rejects the request rather than silently falling back to best-effort — e.g. a
critical CoAP option (RFC 7252 §5.4.1).

This reserves the architectural slot only. **No option or parameter is defined or
registered, and there are no new IANA registrations in this revision.**

## WI-3 — NMDA scoping

Sections: §2.4 Unified datastore; §2 architecture intro; §5.2.1.

Chose to expand the existing §2.4 rather than add a new section — smaller diff,
and that section already carried the single-datastore statement.

- §2.4: CORECONF operates on a single conceptual datastore (the server's applied
  configuration and operational state); selection among NMDA datastores is out of
  scope; a future extension may define datastore selection (e.g. a query
  parameter or URI structure) without changing the semantics defined here.
- §2 architecture intro: "content of datastore(s)" → "content of the datastore".
- §5.2.1: removed the sentence pointing at NMDA for "other examples of
  datastores", which cited [RFC7950] and implied multiple datastores.

**Deviation from plan worth reviewing:** RFC 8342 is kept as a **normative**
reference, not downgraded to informative, because the YANG module imports
`ietf-datastores`. Flagging it explicitly since the opposite was expected.

## WI-4 — Security Considerations

Section: §7. Added a paragraph on the risk introduced by partial application:
a multi-item request that fails midway can leave the datastore in a state the
client did not intend, and clients need to detect and repair that. No new
top-level Operational Considerations section was created.

## WI-5 — Editorial fallout

Abstract and §1: one sentence each noting that atomic/transaction semantics for
multi-item requests and NMDA datastore selection are out of scope and deferred.
No citations in the Abstract, per RFC abstract rules.

## Flagged, deliberately not changed

- §2 architecture figure label "Datastore(s) (5)" (aasvg ASCII art) — left as-is
  to avoid disturbing figure alignment for a cosmetic "(s)".
- §5.1 YANG library: "This module also contains the list of datastores
  implemented." Left as-is — it describes the generic YANG-library discovery
  mechanism, which returns a one-element list under the single-datastore model.
  Not a hard contradiction; edit deferred to avoid scope creep.

## Notes

- Branched from `main` (`f9f19d9`) and independent of #25 — either can
  merge first.
- Whichever of the two merges second will hit a one-line conflict in the iPATCH
  paragraph, where this PR's "processed as described in Section 3.2.1" sentence
  sits next to the other PR's absence-marker sentence. Both sentences survive;
  keep them adjacent.
- Builds clean with `kdrfc draft-ietf-core-comi.md` (aasvg on PATH), no new
  xml2rfc warnings, all cross-references resolve.

comments.author: vvilimek
comments.body:
Hi Andy, Peter and Alexander,

maybe we should explain the motivation behind this PR more. I think that the atomic request processing is too resource-heavy for constrained devices. There are two simple solutions how to fix the CORECONF so that the atomicity is not required:
 - We make the `iPATCH` optional, describing the expected error for implementations not supporting atomic request processing for multiple instances.
 - We relax the `iPATCH` requirements so that they are simpler and less resource-heavy.

I chose the latter solution. 

The fact that the CoAP methods `PATCH` and `iPATCH` require atomic semantics was not known to me when I presented this proposal at IETF 126. Good catch Andy, thanks for your deep review. Because the `iPATCH` MUST be atomic, we should pivot to using method like `POST`. This change should be check to prevent collisions with other types of operations.

@petervanderstok wrote:
> I don't see how a sequence of operations can be atomic without rollback.

The new proposal is that these operations should not be atomic.

@petervanderstok wrote:
> Does ComI support atomicity over a series of operations. I hope not.

I am not sure what are you talking about. What is Coml?

## Error handling
The error handling specification should definitely be better.

comments.author: abierman
comments.body:
I do not support returning success to the client if the server knows it did not perform all the edits correctly.
YANG standards and implementation for edit transactions are complex and intentionally fuzzy.
NETCONF provides (optional) rollback but it is mandatory to implement all-or-none.

NMDA handles real-world distributed system issues such as the delay between making
a configuration change and completing the system changes (convergence).

The server SHOULD:
1) validate all the edits as acceptable
2) apply them to the system in some implementation-specific manner
- returning success should mean no errors detected (yet) by the server
- returning an error means the system may be altered (but the server SHOULD attempt to avoid this state)

comments.author: vvilimek
comments.body:
Hi Andy, Peter and Alexandr,

@abierman wrote:
https://github.com/core-wg/comi/pull/24#issuecomment-5106964792
>I do not support returning success to the client if the server knows it did not perform all the edits correctly.

I agree. Generally the document is not too verbose around errors.

>YANG standards and implementation for edit transactions are complex and intentionally fuzzy.
NETCONF provides (optional) rollback but it is mandatory to implement all-or-none.

Why is it fuzzy _intentionally_? To make life of the programmers easier?

>NMDA handles real-world distributed system issues such as the delay between making
a configuration change and completing the system changes (convergence).

How? I thought that the NMDA is focused on specifying the conceptual (configuration) datastores
on a single server.

>
>The server SHOULD:
>1) validate all the edits as acceptable
>2) apply them to the system in some implementation-specific manner
>- returning success should mean no errors detected (yet) by the server
>- returning an error means the system may be altered (but the server SHOULD attempt to avoid this state)

I am not sure about the numbered points, I agree with the bullet points.


@petervanderstok wrote:
https://github.com/core-wg/comi/pull/24#issuecomment-5107443131
>Hi andy,
>
> Quite a lot of traffic about coreconf.
> Are there actually any users who want to use it?

We in the CZ.NIC are interested.

>
>
> Cheerio,
>
> Peter


@abierman wrote:
https://github.com/core-wg/comi/pull/24#issuecomment-5133885420
>The draft should clarify:
>
>- returning success for an edit operation means the configuration changes are acceptable
   according to the YANG model.

Somewhere on a mailing-list related to NETMOD / NETCONF I encountered a message that
some YANG implementation returns OK status followed by an error. Great design indeed.
I want to avoid this and specify the errors so that it is obvious what happened. What
did go through and what did not.

>- the requested changes are not required to be active in the operational state immediately

Ok, why not. I am not sure how this fits into the RESTful architecture.
I thought that the REST would wait until the thing is done, i.e. the operational state
reflects the config. We might find that it would be better if CORECONF would be closer to NETCONF,
not RESTCONF.

>- this is not 'best-effort', but rather treated as an implementation detail.  It depends on
   the YANG model and the server and the system the server supports.

It is in some sense 'best-effort', you try to apply the writes one by one.
The server may refuse to perform the write because consistency or semantic requirement would get broken.
If a write fails, we continue to the next request element.

Image a situation you want to push as much configuration to a device as possible.
We are configuration 5 independent ratios. If configuration of the first one fails,
we don't care that much. At least the remaining four will be configured.

>- the desired configuration does not change if some parts of it cannot be applied because
   of system issues

I think that the CORECONF should be designed in such way it can fit on MCU like Atmega used by
Arduino. Also the systems should be, in most cases, really simple like a smart light bulb
allowing brightness and RGB colors intesity to be set.
You do not want to implement any kind of rollbacking not such constrained device.
Such device do not care about
consistency.

Or we should add text like: The server should try to prevent
inconsistent state.

I think this part is connected to this issue:
https://github.com/core-wg/comi/pull/24#discussion_r3650440430

I am advocating for such because I want to let us keep the CORECONF as simple as
possible (see my note about Arduinos). The consistency issues should be explained better.

>- Future work: the NMDA operational version of the configuration is used by the client to debug
   non-convergence issues

If such version is available.

comments.author: abierman
comments.body:
```Why is it fuzzy intentionally? To make life of the programmers easier?```

I guess so.
A server can be a distributed system (e.g. main server + subsystems).

Consider a simple 'backup' command.
Does return OK mean the backup request has been accepted and queued?
Does it mean the backup has been started?
Does it mean the backup has finished?
Usually, the data model does not say, so the implementation can do whatever it wants.

The error handling details for iPATCH are clear enough.
CORECONF cannot ignore selected parts of this RFC.

comments.author: abierman
comments.body:
```Are there actually any users who want to use it?```

YumaWorks is interested, but it is not a high priority.
The landscape is changing. Some standards work in progress:

-  UDP-Notif telemetry
-  NETCONF over QUIC
-  RESTCONF over QUIC
-  YANG/CBOR encoding for RESTCONF
-  YANG/CBOR encoding for UDP-Notif

We already support YANG Push in XML, JSON, and CBOR.
YANG/CBOR is a high priority for many organizations.

IMO CORECONF is a great SNMP replacement, supporting
varbind-focused applications needing simple config and monitoring.

reviews.author: abierman
reviews.body:
In general the best-effort approach does not meet iPATCH atomic requirements.
IMO it would be OK to return an error saying partial errors occurred, but not OK
to return OK and the server be silent about the errors.

comments.body:
sec 3.2.3.1 shows an iPATCH example where 3 data nodes are being edited at once.
iPATCH is atomic so why doesn't this count?

RESTCONF uses YANG Patch (RFC 8072) to provide an ordered sequence of edits.
It is implementation-specific how the datastores are used but it is important because of
cross references like leafref.  The draft could say the order of edits within an iPATCH MUST be followed

This is confusing (see previous comment about iPATCH)

A concrete example of what NMDA support might look like can be found in RFC 8527.

the datastore(s) might be more accurate.
RESTCONF takes the position that the server will deal with its datastores as an implementation detail.
Similar hand-waving could apply to CORECONF. iPATCH provides all-or-none semantics.
It is up to the server how that is accomplished.

this is an important definition
The term 'conceptual datastore' might be better than datastore(s)

This seems to contradict text in RFC 8132

```
   PATCH and iPATCH are both atomic.  The server MUST apply the entire
   set of changes atomically and never provide a partially modified
   representation to a concurrently executed GET request.  Given the
   constrained nature of the servers, most servers will only execute
   CoAP requests consecutively, thus preventing a concurrent partial
   overlapping of request modifications.  In other words, modifications
   MUST NOT be applied to the server state when an error occurs or when
   only a partial execution is possible on the resources present in the
   server.
```

It is not possible for the client to be responsible for transaction validation.
Rollback in NETCONF is optional to implement but widely supported because it is needed.

The server needs to return an error if any parts of the edit failed.
The client is still responsible for figuring out how to fix the unapplied config.

You mean an option that says the server MUST implement iPATCH correctly?
IMO iPATCH cannot be changed to ignore MUST requirements.

pulls.title: Use CBOR undefined (0xf7), not null, as the absence/removal marker
pulls.author: apelov
pulls.body:
## Problem

The draft uses CBOR `null` (0xf6) as the absence/removal marker in the
instance-value position. But `null` is exactly how a leaf of type `empty` is
encoded — see [RFC 9254, Section 6.11](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9254#name-the-empty-type).
The marker is therefore indistinguishable from a legitimate value, which breaks
two operations:

- **iPATCH**: an `empty` leaf can never be created or set. `{SID: null}` must be
  interpreted as a deletion of that leaf.
- **FETCH**: an instantiated `empty` leaf cannot be distinguished from a data
  node that is absent or not supported by the server — both come back as `null`.

## Fix

Use CBOR `undefined` (0xf7) as the absence marker. RFC 9254 assigns no meaning
to 0xf7 anywhere, so there is no collision with any YANG type encoding.

The rule and its rationale are now stated **once**, in the
`application/yang-instances+cbor-seq` media-type definition:

> In the position of an instance-value, the CBOR undefined value (0xf7) does not
> carry a value of the data node; it indicates the absence of a value. Its
> precise meaning depends on the method, as specified in Section 3.1.3 and
> Section 3.2.5. The CBOR null value (0xf6) is not used for this purpose: null is
> a valid instance-value for a leaf of type 'empty' (see Section 6.11 of
> [RFC9254]) and can therefore not be distinguished from an absence marker.

The method-specific sections then say only what absence means for that method.
Six sites in total: the media-type definition (iPATCH clause), FETCH, the iPATCH
prose, the iPATCH example, and the empty RPC output example.

Precedent: RFC 7951 §6.9 encodes `empty` as `[null]` in YANG-JSON for exactly
this reason.

## ⚠️ This is a breaking wire change

Against -21, and it fails silently in one direction:

- An old server receiving `undefined` rejects the request as malformed.
- An old client mis-parses a new FETCH response.

Acceptable pre-RFC, but it should be called out to the WG explicitly rather than
left to be discovered in the diff.

## One editorial judgement call

The empty-RPC-output example (§3.5.1, `{ 61000: null }` → `{ 61000: undefined }`)
does **not** collide — an RPC output is always a map, never a bare `null`. It was
changed for consistency, so that there is a single uniform rule ("0xf7 = no value
here") rather than two sentinels whose meaning depends on context. This hunk can
be reverted independently if the WG prefers.

## Noted but deliberately not added to the draft

Generic CBOR→JSON transcoding (RFC 8949 §6.1) maps `undefined` to JSON `null`,
which reintroduces the ambiguity across a transcoding proxy. Left out to keep the
diff minimal — raising it here in case a reviewer asks.

## Notes

- Branched from `main` (`f9f19d9`) and independent of #24 — either can
  merge first.
- Whichever of the two merges second will hit a one-line conflict in the iPATCH
  paragraph, where this PR's `undefined` sentence sits next to the other PR's
  "processed as described in Section 3.2.1" sentence. Both sentences survive;
  keep them adjacent.
- Builds clean with `kdrfc draft-ietf-core-comi.md` (aasvg on PATH), no new
  xml2rfc warnings, all cross-references resolve.

comments.author: petervanderstok
comments.body:
HI,
I don't see all the implications of your suggestion.
However, may I suggest a short version of your motivation section

 In the position of an instance-value, the CBOR undefined value (0xf7) indicates the absence of a value.
  Its precise meaning depends on the method, as specified in
  {{fetch}} and {{ipatch-operation}}.
  The CBOR null value (0xf6) is a valid
  instance-value for a leaf of type 'empty' (see {{Section 6.11 of -yang-cbor}}).

comments.author: vvilimek
comments.body:
Hi,

in principle I agree. This is a good proposition. However not all of the text is correct: 

> - FETCH: an instantiated empty leaf cannot be distinguished from a data
node that is absent or not supported by the server — both come back as null.

Is not true because if you FETCH a `empty` typed leaf, the server:
 - supports it and the leaf is instantiated -> a `SID`, `null` pair is used
 - supports it and the leaf is **NOT** instantiated -> the pair is not present
 - does not support the leaf -> either an error is returned or pair missing in output

## Breaking change
Yes but this is still draft, changes are expected.

## JSON compatibility
The problem of transformation data from YANG-CBOR to YANG-JSON and back requires knowledge of the model (from compiled YANG modules). Nothing new.

## One editorial judgement call
> The empty-RPC-output example (§3.5.1, { 61000: null } → { 61000: undefined })
does not collide — an RPC output is always a map, never a bare null. It was
changed for consistency, so that there is a single uniform rule ("0xf7 = no value
here") rather than two sentinels whose meaning depends on context. This hunk can
be reverted independently if the WG prefers.

I am not sure about this, we should discuss. I would suggest using empty CBOR map for `input`s and `output`s without child data nodes. This should simplify the implementations as the handling is more similar to cases with non-empty `input`s. (The encoding uses 1 byte, same as the `null` or `undefined`).

pulls.title: Specify how a SID is encoded in a URI path segment
pulls.author: apelov
pulls.body:
## Problem

The draft uses a SID-to-URI-path encoding that it never specifies.

Discovery examples return `</c/kv>` (§5.1), `</c/a6>` and `</c/a7>` (§5.2.2). §5.1 says the
YANG library SID 2351 becomes `kv` "after encoding as specified in Section 2.2" — but §2.2
only says that SIDs are numeric identifiers. Grepping the source for `base64`,
`percent-encod` or `path segment` returns nothing.

This is load-bearing for interop, not cosmetic: a `core.c.dn` discovery response carries no
SID attribute, so a client has to decode `a6` back to 1722 to learn which data node a link
refers to.

## Why this misleads rather than merely slowing an implementer down

The scheme is a **positional base-64 numeral** — the SID's binary value cut into 6-bit digits
— *not* base 64 applied to an octet string. Both natural readings of "base64 the SID" give a
different, wrong answer:

| Reading | SID 2351 gives | |
|---|---|---|
| Positional base-64 numeral (what the draft's examples use) | `kv` | ✅ |
| base64url of the raw bytes `0x092f` | `CS8` | ❌ |
| base64url of the CBOR encoding `0x19092f` | `GQkv` | ❌ |

The positional reading reproduces all three examples in the draft and round-trips:
`kv`→2351, `a6`→1722, `a7`→1723.

Note that `GQkv` ends in `kv`, so a reader who tries the CBOR variant gets something that
looks tantalisingly close and is still wrong.

## Second gap: the alphabet is not pinned down by any example

The digit values appearing across all the draft's examples are 26, 36, 47, 58 and 59 — all
below 62. Since base 64 and base 64url differ only at digits 62 and 63 (`+`/`/` versus
`-`/`_`), **no example in the document distinguishes them.**

The new text states base 64url explicitly. `/` inside a path segment would be fatal, and
`k.rb` in the repo root already uses `Base64.urlsafe_encode64(..., padding: false)`, so this
matches the evidenced intent.

## The change

One new subsection, `2.2.1 SIDs in URIs`. 19 lines added, nothing removed, no example
touched.

It is deliberately added as a *child* of §2.2, so §5.1's existing "as specified in
Section 2.2" cross-reference starts resolving to text that actually specifies the encoding —
with zero change to §5.1.

Side effect: RFC 4648 becomes an actually-used normative reference. Today it is normative but
cited exactly once, in Security Considerations, and never where an encoding is defined.

## Open question for review

The text says leading zero digits `MUST NOT` be emitted, but deliberately says nothing about
whether a receiver has to reject them. Leaving receiver behaviour unstated is the smaller
change; if the WG prefers strictness, add "a client MAY reject a representation containing
leading zero digits."

## Notes

- Branched from `main` (`f9f19d9`), independent of #24 and #25. §2.2 is untouched by both, so
  this should not conflict with either in any merge order.
- Builds clean with `kdrfc draft-ietf-core-comi.md` (aasvg on PATH), no new xml2rfc warnings,
  both new `Section N of [RFC4648]` cross-references resolve.
- `Instance-identifiers` renumbers 2.2.1 → 2.2.2. It is not cross-referenced anywhere, so the
  renumbering is inert.
- This is one finding out of a broader review of the current text. The rest is being taken to
  the co-authors separately rather than filed here.
